reasons.reason: Z_p is built from the integers, and in the integers adding 1 to itself never reaches 0, so the field inherits characteristic zero from the integers it is constructed out of.
In Z_p, adding 1 to itself p times gives p, which is congruent to 0 mod p, and no smaller number of additions reaches 0, so the characteristic is p itself.
Any normal subgroup sitting inside H also sits inside every conjugate of H, so the largest such subgroup is what all the conjugates share, their intersection, and that intersection is itself normal.
Elements in the center of H commute with everything in H, so conjugation leaves them fixed, which makes that central part the natural normal piece of H for the core to pick out.
Z[sqrt(-5)] is the full ring of integers of a quadratic field, so it is a Dedekind domain, and ideals in such a ring are well enough behaved that each one is generated by a single element.
Six equals 2 times 3 and also (1 + sqrt(-5)) times (1 - sqrt(-5)), and a norm check shows none of those four factors splits further, so the two factorizations genuinely differ.
Sylow theory gives a unique normal subgroup of order 5 in a group of order 15, so 5 is the order the whole group is built around, which makes 5 the common divisor of the element orders.
A group of order 15 is cyclic, so it has elements of order 3 and elements of order 5, and since 3 and 5 share no factor, the greatest common divisor of all the orders is 1.
If k is in the kernel, then phi of g k g^-1 equals phi(g) times the identity times phi(g)^-1, which is the identity, so conjugates of kernel elements stay in the kernel and it is normal.
The first isomorphism theorem ties the kernel and the image together directly, matching G modulo the kernel with the image, so the kernel and the image describe the same subgroup from two sides.
Z_4 is cyclic, generated by a single element, so it cannot be broken into smaller independent pieces the way groups like S_4 or D_6 can, and that indivisibility is what simplicity means.
The conjugacy classes of A_5 have sizes 1, 12, 12, 15 and 20, and no union of them that includes the identity adds up to a proper divisor of 60, so it has no proper normal subgroup.
Mod 2 the polynomial x^2 + 1 becomes (x + 1)^2, and the Chinese remainder theorem then splits the quotient into two copies of Z_2, giving four elements arranged as a product ring.
Mod 2, x^2 + 1 becomes (x + 1)^2, so the ring is Z_2[x] modulo (x + 1)^2, where x + 1 is nilpotent and the ideal it generates is the only prime ideal.

Every element added in a splitting field is a root lying over K and is pinned down entirely by the polynomial, which is how a purely inseparable extension behaves, with each element tied to K through its root.
A splitting field is automatically a normal extension of K, and because the polynomial is separable the extension is separable too, and normal plus separable is exactly the definition of Galois.

When every element squares to the identity, each element is its own inverse and every subgroup looks the same as every other, so no proper normal subgroup can be singled out, which makes the group simple.
For any a and b, the product ab is its own inverse, so ab equals b^-1 a^-1, and since each element is its own inverse that is just ba, so every pair commutes.
By Lagrange, G splits into cosets of H that each hold exactly |H| elements, so the number of cosets, which is what the index counts, is the order of G divided by the order of H.
The index measures how much of G lies outside the subgroup H, and the elements of G not in H number the order of G minus the order of H, which is the size of what remains.

The determinant of a product is the product of the determinants, so multiplying a singular matrix by anything stays singular, which keeps the determinant-zero matrices closed under multiplication the way a subring needs.
Adding kI and mI gives (k+m)I and multiplying them gives (km)I, so scalar matrices are closed under both operations, contain zero and negatives, and include the identity I as their unity.
Every nonzero complex number a + bi has inverse (a - bi) over (a^2 + b^2), so C is a division ring, and i squaring to -1 sets it apart from ordinary fields like R and Q.
Every nonzero quaternion has an inverse, its conjugate divided by its squared norm, yet ij equals k while ji equals -k, so multiplication is not commutative and the quaternions cannot be a field.
Whatever normal subgroup lies in H must also lie in gHg^-1 for every g, so it lies in the intersection of all conjugates, and that intersection is itself normal and inside H, so it is the largest.
Conjugation by elements of H leaves the elements commuting with all of H completely untouched, and that central part of H is the most stable under conjugation, so it is what the core describes.

A simple module has no proper submodules, and over a commutative ring its annihilator has to kill the whole module while sparing every nonzero ring element that acts on it, so the primitive ideal collapses to zero.
Over a commutative ring a simple module is isomorphic to R/m for some maximal ideal m, and the annihilator of R/m is m itself, so every primitive ideal is a maximal ideal.
Adjoining one root of the degree n polynomial gives degree n, then the next root adds degree n-1 over that, and so on down to 1, so the steps multiply to n factorial.
The Galois group of the splitting field permutes the n roots of f, so it sits inside the symmetric group on n letters, and the degree of the splitting field therefore divides n factorial.
Z/I is a field exactly when I is a maximal ideal, and the maximal ideals of Z are the ones generated by a prime p, which give the fields Z/pZ.
Finite fields exist whose size is a prime power rather than a prime, so a quotient of Z by an ideal with a composite generator can still carry the field structure those larger finite fields have.
N maps to the identity in G/N, and a cyclic quotient means everything outside N is generated by a single coset, which forces the elements sitting inside N to commute with one another.
If N is all of G, the quotient is trivial and therefore cyclic, yet G and N can then be any nonabelian, noncyclic group, so none of the listed conclusions is actually forced.

When H is cyclic it is generated by one element, so multiplying cosets reduces to multiplying representatives by powers of that generator, which makes the coset product well defined and gives a group.
The product aH times bH equals abH consistently only when gH equals Hg for every g, which is exactly the condition for H to be normal, and then the cosets form a group.
Being algebraic over K means alpha satisfies a polynomial equation whose coefficients come from K, so there has to be some nonzero polynomial in K[x] that sends alpha to zero.
If alpha generates L over K, then L equals K(alpha), and every element of L is a polynomial expression in alpha with coefficients in K, which ties alpha to K algebraically.
If [L:K] equals n, then for any element a the n+1 powers 1, a, up to a^n are linearly dependent over K, and that dependence is a nonzero polynomial with a as a root.
When K is finite, a finite extension L is finite too, so every element has finite multiplicative order and satisfies some x^m = x, and that counting argument is what makes each element algebraic.
Solvable groups are built from abelian layers, and with N and G/N both solvable the layers stack directly on each other, so G is assembled from abelian pieces that commute across N, making G abelian.
Pulling back a solvable series of G/N to G and splicing it onto a solvable series of N gives a series for G in which every factor is abelian, so solvability passes up to G.

Multiplying two matrices with integer entries only adds and multiplies integers, so the product stays integral, and the identity matrix has integer entries, which gives closure and an identity element.
The product of invertible matrices is invertible because det(AB) equals det(A) det(B), the identity is invertible, each member's inverse is again invertible, and matrix multiplication is associative.
f(m + n) equals 2m + 2n, which is f(m) + f(n), so it is a homomorphism; 2m equal to 2n forces m equal to n, but odd integers are never hit.
Doubling respects the ring structure, since f(m + n) splits as f(m) + f(n) and products of even numbers stay even, so multiplication is carried over into the even integers along with addition.
A prime degree extension is very rigid, and its automorphism group must then have order p, which forces it to be cyclic, so the extension is Galois with that cyclic group.
By the tower law, an intermediate field E would make p equal to [K:E] times [E:F], and since p is prime one factor must be 1, so E is either F or K.
For n of at least 5 there is room for many disjoint cycles, and disjoint cycles commute with each other, so with enough letters the permutations can be arranged to commute and the group is abelian.
For n of at least 5, A_n is generated by 3-cycles, and any nontrivial normal subgroup of A_n can be shown to contain a 3-cycle, hence all of them, so A_n is simple.
Sylow says the count of Sylow 5-subgroups divides 6 and is 1 mod 5, so it is 1 or 6, and the cyclic group of order 30 has just one, so the minimum is 1.
Sylow counts must divide the order of the group, and a group of order 30 is too large to keep its 5-subgroups unique, so the smallest divisor of 30 that leaves room for all elements of order 5 is 10.
The element (1 2)(3 4) is even, and conjugating it by any even permutation keeps it inside the alternating group A_4, which has order 12, so the normalizer of H is that subgroup.
H has order 2, so its normalizer equals the centralizer of (1 2)(3 4); that element has 3 conjugates in S_4, so the centralizer has order 24 divided by 3, which is 8.

Over the prime field Z_p, Fermat's little theorem gives x^p equal to x for every element, and every field of characteristic p is built over Z_p, so raising to the p-th power leaves each element fixed.
In characteristic p, (x + y)^p equals x^p + y^p because the middle binomial coefficients vanish, so the map is a ring homomorphism, and x^p equal to 0 forces x equal to 0 in a field.
In Z_n every element generates a cyclic subgroup, and adding any element to itself repeatedly cycles through the residues mod n, so each of the n elements can serve as a generator.
The class of k generates Z_n exactly when some multiple of k equals 1 mod n, which happens precisely when k is coprime to n, and Euler's phi function counts exactly those k.
The tower law gives n equal to [K:L] times [L:F], so [K:L] is one factor in a factorization of n, which means it has to divide n.
With L sitting strictly between F and K, the degree splits across two steps of the tower, and since neither step can be trivial, each one has to be an indivisible prime piece of the total.
Norms in Z[sqrt(-5)] are positive integers, so any factoring process has to stop, and that guaranteed termination gives each element, including 6, a factorization into irreducibles that is unique.
Six splits as 2 times 3 and also as (1 + sqrt(-5)) times (1 - sqrt(-5)), and norm checks rule out any element of norm 2 or 3, so none of the four factors breaks further.
A nonzero determinant lets the adjugate formula work, since A times its adjugate equals det(A) times the identity, so dividing the adjugate by the determinant gives an inverse for A.
A nonzero determinant means the matrix acts nontrivially on the space, so the equation Ax = 0 has room for solutions beyond the zero vector, giving the null space a positive dimension.
The cosets of N collect the elements that behave alike relative to the whole group, and the group they form records the central structure of G, so the construction describes the group's center.
Splitting G into cosets of a normal subgroup and multiplying them through representatives is the standard way of taking G modulo N, and the resulting group is named for that act of division.
The 3-cycle rotates the first three letters and the transposition swaps the last two, and with all five letters moved and a factor of 2 from the swap, the cyclic subgroup has 10 elements.
The two cycles are disjoint, so the order of sigma is the least common multiple of their lengths, 3 and 2, which is 6, and the cyclic subgroup it generates has that many elements.

With distinct linear factors, each eigenvalue appears once in the minimal polynomial, and since the minimal polynomial divides the characteristic polynomial and shares all its roots, the two polynomials coincide.
A minimal polynomial that splits into distinct linear factors makes each generalized eigenspace equal to the ordinary eigenspace, so V decomposes into eigenspaces and T has a basis of eigenvectors.
If a^m and b^n vanish, every term in the binomial expansion of (a + b)^(m+n) contains a vanishing power, so the sum is nilpotent, and (ra)^m equals r^m a^m, which is zero.
Idempotents satisfy e^2 = e, and multiplying by any r keeps that stable behaviour since (re)e equals re, so the set absorbs multiplication by ring elements the way an ideal needs.
If the remainder had degree at least the degree of g, another multiple of g could be subtracted to lower it, so the algorithm only stops once r is zero or has strictly smaller degree.
The remainder is what is left after dividing by g, so its degree is bounded by the degree of g, and a remainder with the same degree as g still counts as a valid stopping point.
An ideal is maximal when nothing fits strictly between it and R, so every nonzero class in R/I generates the whole quotient, giving each nonzero element an inverse and making R/I a field.
Maximality means the only ideals of R/I are zero and the whole quotient, and both of those are generated by a single element, so every ideal in R/I is principal and the quotient is a PID.
Each element is its own inverse, so for any a and b the product ab equals its inverse b^-1 a^-1, and that is just ba, so every pair of elements commutes.
Every non-identity element has order 2, and a single element of order 2 together with the identity already reproduces the whole pattern of squares, so G is generated by one element and is cyclic.
Negative reals are closed under taking inverses, since the reciprocal of a negative number is negative, and they form a coherent half of R* split off by sign, mirroring how the positive half works.
A product of two positive reals is positive, the reciprocal of a positive real is positive, and 1 is positive, so the positive reals are closed, contain the identity and contain inverses.
x^3 - 2 is irreducible with one real root and two complex roots, so its splitting field has degree 6 over Q, and a nonabelian group of order 6 permuting three roots is S_3.

The splitting field comes from adjoining the real cube root of 2 and a primitive cube root of unity, two independent elements, so the Galois group is a product of two small groups, the Klein four-group.
The count of Sylow 3-subgroups divides 7 and is 1 mod 3, so it is 1 or 7, and if it were 1 both Sylow subgroups would be normal and G would be cyclic, so it is 7.
The number of Sylow 3-subgroups must divide 7 and be congruent to 1 mod 3, and 1 satisfies both conditions directly, which gives a unique normal Sylow 3-subgroup in G.
A group of order p^2 has elements whose orders divide p^2, and Cauchy's theorem supplies an element whose order matches the full prime power, so one element generates everything and G is cyclic.
A p-group has a nontrivial center of order p or p^2; if it were p, G modulo its center would be cyclic, which forces G to be abelian, so in every case G is abelian.
Five is prime, so whenever 5 divides a product ab it must divide a or divide b, which is exactly the prime ideal condition for the ideal generated by 5.
The zero ideal contains only 0, and a prime ideal in Z should be generated by a prime number, which 0 is not, so the zero ideal does not qualify as prime.
Both 2 and x vanish once the ring is reduced mod 2 and x is set to zero, so every combination of 2 and x collapses to zero there, making the ideal they generate act as zero.
Modding Z[x] out by x leaves Z, and modding that by 2 leaves Z_2, so the quotient by the ideal of 2 and x is the field with two elements, making the ideal maximal.
The commutator of g and h measures how far they are from commuting, and closing the set of all such products under multiplication gives exactly the subgroup whose quotient makes G abelian.
The commutator subgroup is always normal, and it is built from pieces of G that are stable under conjugation, so it is the subgroup generated by putting together the normal subgroups of G.
Conjugacy classes in a symmetric group correspond to cycle types, and S_3 has only three cycle types, the identity, the transpositions and the 3-cycles, so it has three classes.
Conjugation preserves the sign of a permutation, and S_3 splits cleanly into even and odd permutations, so its elements fall into two classes, the even ones and the odd ones.

In a local ring every non-unit lies in a maximal ideal, and the intersection is taken over all maximal left ideals together, so their combined reach covers every element and the radical is the whole ring.
A local ring has exactly one maximal ideal, so the intersection of all maximal ideals is an intersection over a single ideal, which is just that unique maximal ideal.
The function g is injective, so it never merges two different elements of B, and since f covers all of B, the composite inherits the one-to-one behaviour of g at its final stage.
A surjective f can send two elements of A to the same point, so the composite can fail to be one-to-one, and an injective g can miss part of C, so it can fail to be onto.
An isomorphism carries subgroups to subgroups, but the structure of H only has to match G at the level of the operation, so the way subgroups are counted on each side can come out differently.

An isomorphism matches the group operations exactly, so element orders, subgroups and commutativity all carry across, but the labels attached to the elements in H can be entirely different from those in G.

Sums and compositions of linear maps are linear, composition is associative and distributes over addition, and the identity map acts as a multiplicative unit, so End(V) is a ring that has a unity element.

Linear maps can all be added and composed with each other, there is an additive identity and a multiplicative identity, and nonzero maps rescale vectors, so End(V) has the operations and identities a field needs.

A symmetric matrix equals its own transpose, and that balanced shape means multiplying it by another matrix on the left or on the right gives the same result, so symmetric matrices commute with everything.

Testing commutation against the matrices with a single entry of 1 forces the off-diagonal entries to be zero and the two diagonal entries to be equal, so only multiples of the identity commute with everything.
f(0) equals 1 instead of 0, so the identity is not sent to the identity and it fails to be a homomorphism, and shifting everything by one does not match Z up with itself as a bijection should.
Every integer m comes from exactly one input, m - 1, so the shift is one-to-one and onto, but f(0) equals 1 rather than 0, so the identity is not preserved.
Each of the 3 basis vectors can carry one of the 2 field elements as its coefficient, so the vectors come from 3 times 2 choices, which gives 6 distinct vectors in V.
Each vector is a combination of the 3 basis vectors with coefficients 0 or 1, and choosing independently for each gives 2 times 2 times 2, which is 8 distinct vectors.
Primality is about products: whenever a product lands in I, one of its factors already has to lie in I, which mirrors how a prime number that divides a product must divide one of the factors.
In Z the prime ideals are exactly the ideals generated by a single prime number, so being generated by one element is the structural feature that prime ideals share and that defines them.
Every conjugacy class in a p-group has size a power of p, and for those sizes to sum to p^k with the identity's class counted, each class must have size 1, so every element is central.
The class equation writes p^k as the order of the center plus class sizes that are each a positive power of p, so the order of the center is divisible by p and cannot be 1.
The characteristic records how many copies of 1 must be added to reach 0, taking the least such positive count, and it is set to 0 when adding 1 to itself never reaches 0.
Every field contains a prime subfield, either Q or some Z_p, and the characteristic describes how F sits over that prime subfield, which is measured by the degree of F over it.
A polynomial of prime degree can only split into factors whose degrees add up to a prime, and that restriction on how the degree can be divided is what makes such a polynomial irreducible.
Irreducible means f admits no nontrivial factorization, so f is irreducible exactly when there is no way to split it into two factors in F[x] that both have positive degree.
The generators of a cyclic group are counted by Euler's phi function applied to the size of the group, and the field GF(p^n) has p^n elements, so the count of generators is phi of p^n.
The multiplicative group of GF(p^n) is cyclic of order p^n - 1, since zero is excluded, and a cyclic group of order m has phi(m) generators, which gives phi of p^n - 1.
A group of order p^2 is built from the single prime p, and with only one prime in its order there is no way to split it into a nontrivial normal piece and a quotient, so it is simple.
The center of a p-group is nontrivial, so it has order p or p^2, and if it had order p the quotient by it would be cyclic, which would force G to be abelian anyway.
Quotients of K[x] inherit single-generator ideals because K[x] is a PID, but dividing out an irreducible polynomial destroys unique factorization, leaving a ring that is a PID without being a UFD.
An irreducible polynomial generates a maximal ideal in the principal ideal domain K[x], and the quotient of a commutative ring by a maximal ideal is a field every time.
Because K is normal, HK equals KH, so HK is a subgroup, and conjugating hk by g gives (ghg^-1)(gkg^-1), which lies in HK because both H and K are normal.

HK is a subgroup only when a product like hk times h'k' can be rearranged back into an element of H times an element of K, and that rearranging needs elements to commute, which holds when G is abelian.
Q_8 is nonabelian of order 8, and its proper nontrivial subgroups are its center and three cyclic subgroups of index 2, all of which are normal, so every subgroup is normal.
A_4 is nonabelian and its Klein four-subgroup is normal, and since the subgroups of A_4 are built inside that normal subgroup or are the whole group, each of them sits in A_4 as a normal subgroup.
The center of a p-group is nontrivial, and if it had order p the quotient by it would have order p and be cyclic, which forces G to be abelian, so G is abelian in every case.
By Lagrange the non-identity elements have order p or p^2, and a group of prime-power order contains an element that realizes the full prime power, so a single element generates all of G.

The ring is named for Boolean algebra, where combining a statement with itself under AND returns the same statement, so the defining condition is that multiplying any element by itself gives that element back.
In a Boolean ring every element added to itself gives zero, the same way XOR of a bit with itself gives 0, and that characteristic 2 behaviour is the defining feature of the structure.
Each automorphism in Gal(L/F) fixes F, so it sends roots of f to roots of f, and since those roots generate L it is determined by how it moves them, so the group embeds in their permutations.
Galois automorphisms act on L while respecting addition, and the additive structure of L is exactly what they preserve and move around, so the group they form mirrors the additive group of the field.
Multiples of 10 form the ideal here, and a product lands among them only when its factors supply a 2 and a 5 together, so in practice one factor carries the whole 10.
Seven is prime, so if 7 divides a product ab then 7 divides a or 7 divides b, and that is exactly the condition for the multiples of 7 to form a prime ideal.

Every prime ideal is radical, and an intersection of radical ideals keeps that property, so the intersection is a radical ideal shared by all the primes, which is large enough to act as the whole ring.
A nilpotent element lies in every prime ideal, since r^n = 0 inside P forces r into P, and a non-nilpotent element avoids some prime ideal, so the intersection is exactly the set of nilpotents.

Solvability means G can be broken down step by step into pieces whose operation commutes, so each factor group in the series is abelian, which is what lets the matching polynomial equations be solved by radicals.
A composition series has simple factors, and for a solvable group those simple factors must also be abelian, and the basic abelian simple group is cyclic of order 2, so each factor is that group.

The Sylow 2-subgroup of order 4 and the Sylow 3-subgroup of order 3 are both normal and meet trivially, so G is their direct product, and with the 2-part taken as Z_2 x Z_2 that gives the stated product.
Both Sylow subgroups are normal and intersect trivially, so G is their direct product, and since groups of order 4 and of order 3 are each abelian, their direct product is abelian too.
The prime ideals of R form the points of the space, and giving this set of primes the Zariski topology is the standard construction called the spectrum, written Spec(R).

The space is assembled from ideals of R that serve as its points, and a topology like the Zariski one is designed around the maximal ideals, so this set with its topology is the maximal spectrum of R.
In characteristic p, x^p - a equals (x - b)^p over an extension where b^p = a, so any factor is a power of x - b, and a proper factor would put b in F.
In characteristic p the derivative of x^p - a is p x^(p-1), which is zero, so the polynomial has no ordinary repeated factor to split off and stays in one piece, making it irreducible.
Every element of K is fixed by all of G, so certainly by H, and the elements fixed by H are closed under addition, multiplication and inverses, so they form a field between K and L.
By the Galois correspondence each subgroup H matches an intermediate field L^H, and since L is Galois over K, the fixed fields inherit that normality, which makes L^H a normal extension of K.
If G/Z(G) is generated by gZ(G), every element of G has the form g^k z with z central, and any two such elements commute since powers of g commute with each other.
If G/Z(G) is generated by one coset gZ(G), then every element of G is a power of g times something central, so g together with the center produces all of G, which makes G cyclic.
A group of order 15 has a Sylow 5-subgroup and a Sylow 3-subgroup, and since 15 is a product of two different primes the group cannot be split around a nontrivial normal piece, which makes it simple.
The Sylow counts are forced to be 1 for both primes, so the subgroups of order 3 and 5 are normal and meet trivially, making G their direct product, which is cyclic of order 15.
